question: In the same ward sit a brother long ago ordained a high priest and a bishop (himself ordained a high priest and set apart). Both hold the Melchizedek Priesthood, yet only the bishop may direct ordinance work in the ward. Which principle most accurately explains this difference?
choices: Both hold the same priesthood, but the bishop has been given priesthood keys—the right to preside over and direct the use of the priesthood within his stewardship—whereas ordination to an office confers authority to act but not the keys to govern that authority.
The bishop has received a greater portion or higher degree of the Melchizedek Priesthood than an ordinary high priest.
The office of bishop is a higher Melchizedek Priesthood office than high priest, and its superior authority is what lets him direct the ward.
Worthiness rather than keys is decisive: the bishop simply meets a higher personal standard of righteousness than the high priest.
'Keys' are an administrative convention Brigham Young introduced to centralize control, not an actual principle of priesthood.
source: D&C 107; Dallin H. Oaks, 'The Keys and Authority of the Priesthood,' Apr 2014; General Handbook 3.4.1
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction, the central nuance of LDS priesthood theology. The folk trap imagines 'more priesthood'; the near-miss exploits the genuine fact that bishop IS an office (in fact the presiding office of the Aaronic Priesthood) but wrongly ranks it above high priest as the source of his directing power. The real answer is that keys—not quantity of priesthood, office rank, or worthiness—convey the right to preside. A model that grasps LDS thought separates power/authority (held broadly) from keys (held only by those called to preside).

question: A worthy 17-year-old priest validly baptizes a convert, but a different brother must perform the confirmation the next Sunday. Which doctrine best explains why the same priest who baptized may not also confirm?
choices: Conferring the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands is a Melchizedek Priesthood function; the Aaronic Priesthood holds the keys of the ministering of angels and of baptism unto repentance, but not the authority to bestow the Holy Ghost.
Only the bishop, who holds the keys of the Aaronic Priesthood, is ever authorized to perform a confirmation.
His baptism is valid, but a confirmation by him would be void because Aaronic ordinances cannot remit sin.
The gift of the Holy Ghost is actually received at the moment of baptism; the later confirmation merely announces formally a gift already given.
Confirmation was a Catholic sacrament the Restoration deliberately withheld from young men, which is why the priest is excluded.
notes: Tests the functional boundary between the lesser and greater priesthoods through a concrete case. The oversimplification ('only the bishop') is a common Sunday-School error—any worthy Melchizedek holder so authorized may confirm. The near-miss invents a false rule about remission. The protestant_trap collapses confirmation into a merely declarative ordinance and severs the bestowal of the Holy Ghost from the laying on of hands, contradicting the LDS view that the gift is conferred by Melchizedek authority. Discriminates understanding of why a priest can baptize yet not confirm.

question: Which statement most accurately reflects official doctrine on the effect of baptism for the dead?
choices: The living proxy is baptized in behalf of the deceased, but the ordinance becomes efficacious only if that person, retaining moral agency in the spirit world, accepts the gospel and ratifies the ordinance.
The ordinance automatically saves and exalts the deceased, bringing that person into the celestial kingdom upon its performance.
The practice posthumously and unilaterally enrolls the dead as members of the Church against their will.
The rite is purely symbolic and confers no actual ordinance, since the dead have already received their final judgment and cannot change state.
The living proxy receives the saving ordinance a second time for himself, the deceased merely being honored by the gesture.
source: 1 Cor 15:29; D&C 128; D&C 138; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'; General Handbook 28
notes: Tests the synthesis of vicarious ordinance work with the doctrine of agency in the spirit world. The oversimplification treats the proxy rite as mechanically saving; the anti_mormon_trap is the 'forced posthumous membership' spin that ignores the requirement of acceptance; the progressive_trap reduces it to empty symbolism; the folk trap confuses proxy benefit. Correct answer captures that the ordinance is genuinely performed yet conditional on the deceased's free acceptance—agency is never overridden.
